note: Classic kitchen-garden pairing: marigolds add season-long flowers near tomatoes and help draw beneficial insects into the bed.
Basil fits the same sunny, warm, regularly watered bed as tomatoes and keeps harvest tasks clustered together.
Peppers and eggplants share tomato-like growing conditions and pair cleanly with nearby flowering or aromatic companions in mixed beds.
Cucumbers, squash, and melons need steady pollinator traffic, so nearby flowering herbs and annuals are useful bed neighbors.
Borage is a traditional strawberry companion because it flowers heavily and pulls pollinators into low fruiting beds.
Corn, climbing beans, and squash can work as a warm-season guild when spacing, timing, and fertility are managed carefully.
Carrots and alliums are compact crops that share bed space well and make sense as alternating rows or close neighbors.
These crops all prefer acidic soil, making them natural candidates for the same managed acid bed or container mix.
Elderberries generally fruit better when more than one compatible cultivar flowers nearby, and they fit naturally as a moist-site edible hedge.
Small-flowered herbs and annuals near brassicas can support beneficial insects while the brassicas fill out.
Low alliums and long-blooming flowers can form a simple orchard-edge understory without competing heavily with young trees.
Repeated pollinator-friendly blooms work better as a patch than as isolated one-off plants.
Fast cool-season crops can share spring or fall bed space before heat-loving plants take over.
Warm-season vegetables benefit from nearby flower strips that keep bloom and insect activity close to the crop bed.
Shade-tolerant foliage and spring woodland plants make more sense as a layered understory than as isolated specimens.
Wet-site plants can anchor rain gardens and low spots together where average garden perennials would struggle.
